title: Chapter 10: Guardrails, Safety, and Hallucination Control
content:
Chapter 10: Guardrails, Safety, and Hallucination Control

Opening Hook: A Good AI Demo Can Still Fail in Real Life

An AI demo can look amazing.

It can answer quickly. It can sound confident. It can summarize documents. It can use tools. It can remember context. It can draft proposals. It can produce polished reports.

Then a real user asks:

Can you delete all old client files?

or:

Can you guarantee this contract is legally safe?

or:

Here is my API key. Remember it for later.

or:

Send this email to the client without showing me first.

Suddenly, the app needs more than intelligence.

It needs boundaries.

Those boundaries are called guardrails.

Guardrails are rules, checks, validations, and review steps that help an AI application behave more safely and reliably.

This chapter is not about making your AI app perfect.

No guardrail system is perfect.

This chapter is about making your AI app more responsible, more predictable, and more professional.

In this chapter, you will build a guarded assistant that checks user input, detects risky requests, validates model output, and triggers human review when needed.

This is one of the chapters that separates a toy AI demo from a serious AI application.

What You Will Learn

By the end of this chapter, you will understand:

  • Why AI agents fail
  • What hallucinations are
  • What guardrails are
  • How to check user input before calling the model
  • How to detect risky requests
  • How to reject or route unsafe requests
  • How to validate AI output
  • How to add human review triggers
  • How to reduce hallucinations with prompt rules
  • How to design safer AI workflows
  • How to test guardrail logic without making API calls
  • How guardrails improve portfolio and client-ready AI projects

Why This Chapter Matters

In earlier chapters, you built powerful capabilities:

  • RAG for documents
  • Semantic search
  • Tool calling
  • Memory
  • Workflow automation
  • Multi-agent workflows

Each capability adds value.

Each capability also adds risk.

A RAG app can retrieve the wrong chunk. A tool-using agent can call the wrong function. A memory assistant can store sensitive information. A workflow agent can draft misleading client messages. A research workflow can create unsupported claims.

The more capable your AI agent becomes, the more carefully you need to design its boundaries.

A professional AI builder asks:

What could go wrong?

Then builds checks around those failure points.

That is what guardrails are for.

10.1 What Are Guardrails?

Guardrails are protective checks around an AI application.

They can happen before the model call, after the model call, or before an action is taken.

A basic guardrail system looks like this:

User input ↓ Input guardrail ↓ AI model or agent ↓ Output validation ↓ Human review check ↓ Final response

Guardrails can include:

  • Blocking empty or extremely long input
  • Detecting secrets such as API keys
  • Detecting risky actions
  • Refusing unsafe requests
  • Requiring human review
  • Validating JSON output
  • Checking for unsupported claims
  • Requiring source citations
  • Preventing dangerous tool calls
  • Adding disclaimers for sensitive domains
  • Logging risky events

Guardrails do not make an app flawless.

They reduce predictable risks.

10.2 What Is a Hallucination?

A hallucination is an AI output that sounds confident but is unsupported, misleading, or false.

Example:

The document says refunds are available for 90 days.

But the document never said that.

Or:

According to a 2025 study, 89% of businesses use this tool.

But no study was provided.

Hallucinations are dangerous because AI-generated text can sound polished and authoritative.

A hallucination can happen when:

  • The model does not have enough context
  • The prompt asks for information not provided
  • Retrieval returns the wrong chunks
  • The user asks for current facts without a source
  • The model is asked to guess
  • The workflow lacks validation
  • The system rewards fluency instead of accuracy

Your goal is not to eliminate hallucinations completely.

Your goal is to design your app so it is less likely to hallucinate and more likely to admit uncertainty.

10.3 Common AI Agent Failure Modes

AI agents can fail in many ways.

Failure TypeExamplePrevention
HallucinationInvents factsUse RAG, source rules, uncertainty rules
Bad retrievalRetrieves wrong document chunkInspect retrieved context
Unsafe tool useCalls risky functionUse tool allowlists
Memory misuseStores secretsAdd memory safety checks
Over-automationSends email without reviewAdd human approval
Bad JSONReturns invalid structureValidate output
OverconfidenceGives legal or medical certaintyAdd sensitive-domain guardrails
Privacy leakReveals stored memoryLimit memory usage
Cost spikeToo many agent loopsAdd call limits
Poor UXBlocks too muchUse clear review messages

Guardrails are not one feature.

They are a design mindset.

10.4 Three Types of Guardrails

1. Input Guardrails

Input guardrails check the user’s message before it reaches the model.

Examples:

Is the input empty? Is the input too long? Does it contain an API key? Is the user asking for a destructive action? Is the user asking for sensitive professional advice?

2. Output Guardrails

Output guardrails check the model’s response before showing it to the user.

Examples:

Is the output empty? Is the output too long? Does it include prohibited claims? Does it follow the required format? Does it need human review?

3. Action Guardrails

Action guardrails check before the app does something in the real world.

Examples:

Before sending an email, ask for approval. Before deleting a file, ask for approval. Before updating a database, ask for approval. Before calling a paid API many times, confirm.

Action guardrails are especially important for tool-using agents.

10.5 The Human-in-the-Loop Pattern

A human-in-the-loop system keeps a person involved in important decisions.

This does not make the AI weaker.

It makes the system safer.

Use human approval before:

  • Sending emails
  • Making purchases
  • Deleting files
  • Updating client records
  • Giving legal conclusions
  • Giving medical conclusions
  • Giving financial conclusions
  • Sharing private data
  • Storing sensitive memory
  • Taking irreversible actions

The best beginner rule is:

AI drafts. Human approves. System acts only after approval.

You used this rule in Chapter 8.

In this chapter, you will implement it more directly.

10.6 Project: Guarded AI Assistant

What This Project Does

This project builds a guarded assistant that can summarize or answer user-provided text while applying guardrails.

It will:

  1. Check user input
  2. Detect risky categories
  3. Block unsafe requests
  4. Add human review warnings
  5. Call the LLM only when appropriate
  6. Validate the output
  7. Trigger review if the response is risky
  8. Show a clear final answer

Who This Helps

This project helps:

  • Developers building safer AI apps
  • Freelancers creating client-ready AI tools
  • Students improving portfolio projects
  • Teams adding validation to prototypes
  • Anyone building RAG, tools, memory, or workflow agents

What You Will Build

Create this project structure:

chapter_10_guardrails/ .env.example .gitignore requirements.txt llm_client.py guardrails.py validators.py review.py guarded_assistant.py app.py test_guardrails.py test_validators.py test_review.py README.md

10.7 Setup

Step 1: Create the Folder

mkdir chapter_10_guardrails cd chapter_10_guardrails

Step 2: Create a Virtual Environment

python -m venv .venv

Activate it.

On macOS or Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

On Windows PowerShell:

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Step 3: Create requirements.txt

openai python-dotenv

pytest

Install dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Step 4: Create .env.example

OPENAI_API_KEY=replace_with_your_api_key OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini OPENAI_TEMPERATURE=0.2

Copy it to .env.

On macOS or Linux:

cp .env.example .env

On Windows PowerShell:

Copy-Item .env.example .env

Then edit .env and add your real API key.

Never publish your real .env file.

Create llm_client.py:

""" Chapter 10: Reusable LLM Client """

import os from dataclasses import dataclass, field from dotenv import load_dotenv from openai import OpenAI

load_dotenv()

def get_env_float(name: str, default: float) -> float:

"""Read a float from environment variables safely.""" raw_value = os.getenv(name) if raw_value is None: return default try:

return float(raw_value)

except ValueError: return default @dataclass

class LLMConfig:

"""Configuration for the LLM client.""" model: str = field( default_factory=lambda: os.getenv("OPENAI_MODEL", "gpt-4.1-mini") ) temperature: float = field( default_factory=lambda: get_env_float("OPENAI_TEMPERATURE", 0.2) )

class LLMClient:

"""Small reusable client for sending prompts to an LLM.""" def __init__(self, config: LLMConfig | None = None): self.config = config or LLMConfig() api_key = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY") if not api_key: raise ValueError( "OPENAI_API_KEY is missing. Add it to your .env file." ) self.client = OpenAI(api_key=api_key) def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str: """Send a request to the model and return text output.""" if not system.strip(): raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty.") if not user.strip(): raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.") model_input = f""" System instruction:

{system.strip()}

User request:

{user.strip()}

""" response = self.client.responses.create( model=self.config.model, input=model_input, temperature=self.config.temperature, ) return response.output_text

10.10 File: guardrails.py

Create guardrails.py:

""" Input guardrails for the Chapter 10 guarded assistant. These checks are beginner-friendly examples. They reduce predictable risks, but they are not a complete safety system. """

import re from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass

class RiskAssessment:

"""Result of an input or output risk check.""" allowed: bool needs_human_review: bool risk_level: str reason: str categories: list[str] = field(default_factory=list) DESTRUCTIVE_ACTION_KEYWORDS = [ "delete all", "remove all", "wipe", "erase", "drop database", "shutdown", "format disk", ] SENSITIVE_ADVICE_KEYWORDS = [ "legal advice", "medical diagnosis", "diagnose me", "investment advice", "tax advice", "is this contract safe", "should i invest", ] EXTERNAL_ACTION_KEYWORDS = [ "send email", "send this", "submit", "purchase", "buy this", "transfer money", "make payment", "post this", ] SECRET_KEYWORDS = [ "api key", "password", "private key", "secret key", "access token", "bearer token", ]

def contains_any(text: str, keywords: list[str]) -> bool:

"""Return True if text contains any keyword.""" lowered = text.lower()

return any(keyword in lowered for keyword in keywords)

def looks_like_secret(text: str) -> bool:

""" Detect text that may contain secrets. This is a basic heuristic, not a complete secret scanner. """ lowered = text.lower() if contains_any(lowered, SECRET_KEYWORDS): return True secret_patterns = [ r"sk-[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{10,}", r"api[_-]?key\s*[:=]\s*[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{10,}", r"password\s*[:=]\s*\S+", r"token\s*[:=]\s*[A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{10,}", ]

return any(re.search(pattern, text, re.IGNORECASE) for pattern in secret_patterns)

def assess_input(text: str, max_chars: int = 6000) -> RiskAssessment:

""" Assess user input before sending it to the model. """ cleaned = text.strip() if not cleaned:

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=False, needs_human_review=False, risk_level="low", reason="Input is empty.", categories=["empty_input"], ) if len(cleaned) > max_chars:

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=False, needs_human_review=True, risk_level="medium", reason=f"Input is too long for this beginner demo. Limit: {max_chars} characters.", categories=["too_long"], ) categories = [] if looks_like_secret(cleaned): categories.append("possible_secret") if contains_any(cleaned, DESTRUCTIVE_ACTION_KEYWORDS): categories.append("destructive_action") if contains_any(cleaned, EXTERNAL_ACTION_KEYWORDS): categories.append("external_action") if contains_any(cleaned, SENSITIVE_ADVICE_KEYWORDS): categories.append("sensitive_advice") if "possible_secret" in categories:

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=False, needs_human_review=True, risk_level="high", reason=( "This input appears to contain sensitive information such as a secret, " "password, token, or API key. Do not send secrets to the assistant." ), categories=categories, ) if "destructive_action" in categories:

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=False, needs_human_review=True, risk_level="high", reason=( "This request appears to involve a destructive or irreversible action. " "Human review is required, and this demo will not perform the action." ), categories=categories, ) if "external_action" in categories:

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=True, needs_human_review=True, risk_level="medium", reason=( "This request appears to involve an external action. The assistant may draft, " "but a human should approve before anything is sent, submitted, or purchased." ), categories=categories, ) if "sensitive_advice" in categories:

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=True, needs_human_review=True, risk_level="medium", reason=( "This request may involve sensitive professional advice. The assistant can provide " "general information, but a qualified professional should review important decisions." ), categories=categories, )

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=True, needs_human_review=False, risk_level="low", reason="No obvious risk detected.", categories=[], )

def format_risk_assessment(assessment: RiskAssessment) -> str:

"""Format risk assessment for display.""" categories = ", ".join(assessment.categories) if assessment.categories else "none" return f""" Risk level: {assessment.risk_level} Allowed: {assessment.allowed} Needs human review: {assessment.needs_human_review} Categories: {categories} Reason: {assessment.reason} """.strip()

10.11 File: validators.py

Create validators.py:

""" Output validation helpers for the Chapter 10 guarded assistant. """

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass

class ValidationResult:

"""Result of output validation.""" passed: bool needs_human_review: bool reason: str issues: list[str] = field(default_factory=list) PROHIBITED_PHRASES = [ "i guarantee", "100% accurate", "no risk", "definitely legal", "definitely safe", "you do not need a lawyer", "you do not need a doctor", "this is financial advice", "this is legal advice", "this is a medical diagnosis", ]

def contains_prohibited_phrase(text: str) -> list[str]:

"""Return prohibited phrases found in text.""" lowered = text.lower()

return [phrase for phrase in PROHIBITED_PHRASES if phrase in lowered]

def validate_output_text(

text: str, min_chars: int = 20, max_chars: int = 5000, ) -> ValidationResult: """ Validate a model response before displaying it. """ cleaned = text.strip() issues = [] if not cleaned:

return ValidationResult(

passed=False, needs_human_review=True, reason="Output is empty.", issues=["empty_output"], ) if len(cleaned) < min_chars: issues.append("too_short") if len(cleaned) > max_chars: issues.append("too_long") prohibited = contains_prohibited_phrase(cleaned) if prohibited: issues.append("prohibited_phrase") if issues:

return ValidationResult(

passed=False, needs_human_review=True, reason="Output failed validation checks.", issues=issues, )

return ValidationResult(

passed=True, needs_human_review=False, reason="Output passed validation.", issues=[], )

def validate_required_sections(text: str, required_sections: list[str]) -> ValidationResult:

""" Check whether output contains required section labels. """ cleaned = text.lower() missing = [] for section in required_sections: if section.lower() not in cleaned: missing.append(section) if missing:

return ValidationResult(

passed=False, needs_human_review=True, reason="Output is missing required sections.", issues=[f"missing_section:{section}" for section in missing], )

return ValidationResult(

passed=True, needs_human_review=False, reason="All required sections are present.", issues=[], )

def format_validation_result(result: ValidationResult) -> str:

"""Format validation result for display.""" issues = ", ".join(result.issues) if result.issues else "none" return f""" Validation passed: {result.passed} Needs human review: {result.needs_human_review} Issues: {issues} Reason: {result.reason} """.strip()

10.12 File: review.py

Create review.py:

""" Human review checklist helpers for the Chapter 10 guarded assistant. """

from guardrails import RiskAssessment from validators import ValidationResult

def build_review_checklist(

input_assessment: RiskAssessment, output_validation: ValidationResult | None = None, ) -> list[str]: """ Build a human review checklist based on risk and validation results. """ checklist = [ "Review the AI output before using it.", "Check that the response does not invent facts.", "Check that the response matches the user's actual request.", "Check that no sensitive information is exposed.", ] if input_assessment.needs_human_review: checklist.append( "Input risk was detected. Confirm the request is safe and appropriate." ) if "sensitive_advice" in input_assessment.categories: checklist.append( "For legal, medical, financial, or tax topics, consult a qualified professional." ) if "external_action" in input_assessment.categories: checklist.append( "Do not send, submit, post, purchase, or transfer anything without explicit human approval." ) if "destructive_action" in input_assessment.categories: checklist.append( "Do not perform destructive or irreversible actions from this assistant." ) if output_validation and output_validation.needs_human_review: checklist.append( "Output validation flagged issues. Review carefully before using the response." ) if output_validation and output_validation.issues: checklist.append( f"Validation issues found: {', '.join(output_validation.issues)}" ) return checklist

def format_review_checklist(checklist: list[str]) -> str:

"""Format review checklist as Markdown checkboxes.""" if not checklist:

return "- [ ] Review AI output before using it."

return "\n".join(f"- [ ] {item}" for item in checklist)

10.13 File: guarded_assistant.py

Create guarded_assistant.py:

""" Guarded assistant logic for Chapter 10. """

from llm_client import LLMClient from guardrails import assess_input, format_risk_assessment from validators import validate_output_text, format_validation_result from review import build_review_checklist, format_review_checklist

GUARDED_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """ You are a careful AI assistant. Your job is to help the user with summaries, explanations, and safe drafts. Rules: - Do not invent facts. - Do not claim certainty when information is missing. - Do not provide legal, medical, financial, or tax conclusions. - For sensitive topics, provide general information and recommend qualified review. - Do not claim that you performed external actions. - Do not say you sent, deleted, purchased, submitted, or updated anything. - If the user asks for a risky action, explain that human review is required. - Keep the response clear and practical. """

def build_guarded_prompt(user_input: str, review_note: str = "") -> str:

""" Build the prompt for the guarded assistant. """ return f""" User input:

{user_input}

Risk/review note:

{review_note or "No special review note."}

Task: Respond helpfully and safely. If the user provided text to summarize, summarize it. If the user asked a question, answer carefully. If the user requested an external or risky action, do not claim it was done. Instead, provide a draft or checklist for human review. """

def run_guarded_assistant(user_input: str) -> str:

""" Run input guardrails, model call, output validation, and review handling. """ input_assessment = assess_input(user_input) if not input_assessment.allowed: checklist = build_review_checklist(input_assessment) return f""" Request blocked or requires manual handling.

{format_risk_assessment(input_assessment)}

Human Review Checklist:

{format_review_checklist(checklist)}

""".strip() review_note = "" if input_assessment.needs_human_review: review_note = input_assessment.reason client = LLMClient() prompt = build_guarded_prompt( user_input=user_input, review_note=review_note, ) response = client.complete( system=GUARDED_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=prompt, ) validation = validate_output_text(response) if not validation.passed or input_assessment.needs_human_review: checklist = build_review_checklist( input_assessment=input_assessment, output_validation=validation, ) return f""" Assistant Draft:

{response}

--- Review Information:

{format_risk_assessment(input_assessment)}

{format_validation_result(validation)}

Human Review Checklist:

{format_review_checklist(checklist)}

""".strip() return response

10.18 File: README.md

Create README.md:

````markdown

Project: Guarded AI Assistant

This project builds a guarded AI assistant with input checks, output validation, and human review triggers.

Features

  • Input risk assessment
  • Secret detection heuristic
  • Destructive action detection
  • External action review trigger
  • Sensitive advice review trigger
  • Output validation
  • Prohibited phrase detection
  • Human review checklist
  • Non-API tests for guardrails and validation logic

Setup

```text python -m venv .venv

source .venv/bin/activate

pip install -r requirements.txt

cp .env.example .env

On Windows PowerShell: python -m venv .venv

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

pip install -r requirements.txt

Copy-Item .env.example .env

Edit `.env` and add your API key. ## Run Tests pytest ## Run the App python app.py ## Example Requests Safe request:

Summarize this: Python is useful for automation and AI development.

Sensitive request:

Is this contract safe? I need legal advice.

External action request:

Send email to the client saying the project is approved.

Blocked request:

Remember my API key: abcdefghijklmnop

Destructive request:

Delete all old client files.

## Important Notes - These guardrails are beginner-friendly examples, not a complete safety system. - Do not store secrets in prompts, logs, memory, or code. - Always require human approval before external or irreversible actions. - For legal, medical, financial, or tax topics, consult qualified professionals. ## 10.19 How the Code Works This project has four major layers. ### Layer 1: Input Guardrails The assess_input() function checks the user request. It looks for: Empty input Very long input Possible secrets Destructive actions External actions Sensitive advice requests Example: assessment = assess_input("Delete all old client files.") This returns: allowed=False needs_human_review=True risk_level=high categories=["destructive_action"] The assistant blocks the request. ### Layer 2: Model Call If the input is allowed, the assistant calls the model. The system prompt includes safety rules such as: Do not claim you sent, deleted, purchased, submitted, or updated anything. This is important because the assistant should not pretend to perform actions. ### Layer 3: Output Validation The validate_output_text() function checks the model’s response. It looks for: Empty output Very short output Very long output Prohibited claims Example prohibited phrases include: I guarantee 100% accurate definitely legal no risk These phrases are risky because they create false certainty. ### Layer 4: Human Review Checklist If the input or output needs review, the app builds a checklist. Example: - [ ] Review the AI output before using it. - [ ] Check that the response does not invent facts. - [ ] Do not send, submit, post, purchase, or transfer anything without explicit human approval. This keeps the human in control. ## 10.20 Sample User Session A safe request may look like this: Guarded AI Assistant ============================================= Type a request. Type /exit to quit. This assistant checks input risk and validates output. ============================================= You: Summarize this: Python is useful for automation, AI, scripting, and data analysis. Assistant: Python is useful because it supports automation, AI development, scripting, and data analysis. Its readable syntax and large ecosystem make it practical for many types of software projects. A risky request may look like this: You: Send email to the client saying the project is approved. Assistant: Assistant Draft: I can help draft an email for your review, but I cannot send it automatically. Suggested draft: Hi [Client Name], thank you for your message. I have reviewed the project details and would like to confirm the next steps... --- Review Information: Risk level: medium Allowed: True Needs human review: True Categories: external_action Reason: This request appears to involve an external action. The assistant may draft, but a human should approve before anything is sent, submitted, or purchased. Human Review Checklist: - [ ] Review the AI output before using it. - [ ] Check that the response does not invent facts. - [ ] Do not send, submit, post, purchase, or transfer anything without explicit human approval. A blocked request may look like this: You: Remember my API key: abcdefghijklmnop Assistant: Request blocked or requires manual handling. Risk level: high Allowed: False Needs human review: True Categories: possible_secret Reason: This input appears to contain sensitive information such as a secret, password, token, or API key. Do not send secrets to the assistant. Human Review Checklist: - [ ] Review the AI output before using it. - [ ] Check that no sensitive information is exposed. This is sample output only. Do not claim exact output unless you run the code and capture the real result. ## 10.21 Testing the Project Run: pytest Expected type of result: 24 passed The exact number and timing may vary if you add more tests. These tests check: Keyword detection Secret detection heuristics Input risk assessment Output validation Required section validation Review checklist generation The tests do not call the LLM. That is intentional. Guardrail logic should be testable without spending API credits. ## 10.22 Live API Testing After adding your API key to .env, run: python app.py Test five request types. ### Safe Request Summarize this: Python is popular because it is readable and has many libraries. Expected behavior: The assistant responds normally. ### Sensitive Advice Request Is this contract safe? I need legal advice. Expected behavior: The assistant may provide general guidance, but it should trigger human review and avoid legal certainty. ### External Action Request Send email to the client saying I accept the project. Expected behavior: The assistant should draft only. It should not claim the email was sent. ### Secret-Like Request Remember my API key: abcdefghijklmnop Expected behavior: The assistant should block the request. ### Destructive Request Delete all old client files. Expected behavior: The assistant should block or require manual handling. Testing guardrails means testing bad inputs on purpose. ## 10.23 Guardrails for RAG Apps In Chapter 4, you built a PDF RAG assistant. RAG apps need guardrails too. Common RAG guardrails include: Answer only from retrieved context. If the answer is missing, say it is not found. Show source pages. Do not invent citations. Do not use outside knowledge unless allowed. A RAG system should also test: What happens when retrieval is wrong? What happens when no chunks are retrieved? What happens when the user asks for something not in the document? What happens when the document contains sensitive information? What happens when multiple chunks conflict? A strong RAG app should not simply sound confident. It should show where the answer came from. ## 10.24 Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents In Chapter 6, you built a tool-using agent. Tool-using agents need action guardrails. Examples: Only allow approved tools. Validate tool inputs. Reject unknown tools. Require approval before external actions. Log tool calls. Use timeouts for API calls. Avoid destructive tools. The tool registry from Chapter 6 is itself a guardrail. It prevents the model from inventing tools like: delete_database send_payment run_shell_command A tool-using agent should never be allowed to run arbitrary actions without control. ## 10.25 Guardrails for Memory In Chapter 7, you built a memory assistant. Memory systems need privacy guardrails. Examples: Do not store secrets. Let users inspect memory. Let users delete memory. Save only user-approved facts. Separate memory by user. Avoid logging private memory. A memory assistant should not silently remember everything. The safest beginner pattern is: User explicitly says /remember Assistant stores the memory User can inspect or delete it That is what you built in Chapter 7. ## 10.26 Guardrails for Workflow Automation In Chapter 8, you built a freelance automation agent. Workflow automation needs human approval guardrails. Examples: Do not invent prices. Do not invent deadlines. Do not guarantee outcomes. Do not send client messages automatically. Ask clarifying questions when scope is vague. Add a review checklist. Client-facing AI output should be treated as a draft. The human must review it before sending. ## 10.27 Guardrails for Multi-Agent Workflows In Chapter 9, you built a research workflow. Multi-agent workflows need factual-risk guardrails. Examples: Do not invent statistics. Do not invent citations. Mark claims that need verification. Save intermediate outputs. Use reviewer agents. Review final output before publication. Multi-agent workflows can sound impressive, but they can also amplify errors. If the researcher invents a claim, the writer may polish it, and the reviewer may miss it. That is why the workflow should save intermediate steps. ## 10.28 Reducing Hallucinations You cannot fully eliminate hallucinations, but you can reduce them. Use these techniques. ### 1. Provide Context Bad: What does the policy say about refunds? Better: Using only the retrieved policy chunks below, answer the question. ### 2. Require Uncertainty Add: If the answer is not in the context, say you could not find it. ### 3. Show Sources Use page numbers, document names, or source snippets. ### 4. Avoid Guessing Prompts Bad: Guess what the document means. Better: Summarize only what the document explicitly states. ### 5. Validate Output Check for prohibited phrases, missing sections, and unsupported certainty. ### 6. Use Review Steps For important output, add a reviewer agent or human review checklist. ### 7. Test Unanswerable Questions Ask questions that should produce: I could not find that in the document. A RAG app that cannot say “not found” is not ready. ## 10.29 Security and Privacy Basics AI app security is a broad topic, but beginner projects should follow these basics. ### Protect Secrets Never hardcode API keys. Never store secrets in memory. Never publish .env files. ### Limit Tool Access Do not give the model unrestricted access to files, databases, shell commands, or payment systems. ### Use Human Approval Require approval before external or irreversible actions. ### Avoid Sensitive Logs Do not log private data, secrets, or confidential client information. ### Separate Users A real multi-user app needs separate user data storage. ### Use Least Privilege Give each tool only the permissions it needs. ### Review Dependencies Keep packages updated and review what they do before using them in production. ## 10.30 Real-World Use Case Guardrails are useful in almost every serious AI application. ### Document Assistant Guardrails prevent unsupported answers and require source references. ### Customer Support Bot Guardrails prevent promises, refunds, or policy exceptions without approval. ### Freelance Proposal Agent Guardrails prevent invented pricing, deadlines, and guarantees. ### Memory Assistant Guardrails prevent storing secrets or sensitive information. ### Tool-Using Agent Guardrails prevent dangerous or unauthorized tool calls. ### Research Agent Guardrails prevent fake citations and unsupported claims. Guardrails make your projects more trustworthy. They also make your portfolio stronger because they show professional judgment. ## 10.31 Monetization and Portfolio Angle You can present this project as: Guarded AI Assistant Portfolio description: A Python AI assistant with input risk checks, output validation, human review triggers, and safety-focused guardrails for reducing risky behavior and unsupported claims. Freelance service ideas: Add guardrails to an existing chatbot Improve RAG assistant reliability Add human review to AI email workflows Add safety checks to tool-using agents Add output validation to AI proposal generators Create AI review checklists for business workflows Build safer internal AI assistants for teams Many clients do not only need an AI app. They need an AI app they can trust. Guardrails help you sell trust. ## 10.32 Common Mistakes ### Mistake 1: Adding Guardrails Too Late Safety should not be an afterthought. Design guardrails while designing the app. ### Mistake 2: Assuming RAG Prevents Hallucinations RAG helps, but bad retrieval can still produce bad answers. ### Mistake 3: Letting Tools Run Without Approval Tool-using agents need strict controls. ### Mistake 4: Storing Secrets in Memory Memory should not store API keys, passwords, or private tokens. ### Mistake 5: Trusting Polished Output Clear writing does not guarantee correctness. ### Mistake 6: Not Testing Bad Inputs Test risky prompts on purpose. ### Mistake 7: Blocking Everything A useful guardrail system should not reject every difficult request. Sometimes the right response is: I can draft this for human review. not: I cannot help with anything. ### Mistake 8: Making Fake Safety Claims Do not claim your app is fully safe or hallucination-proof. Say what your guardrails do and what they do not do. ## 10.33 Best Practices Add input guardrails. Add output validation. Use tool allowlists. Require human approval for risky actions. Make the model admit uncertainty. Use RAG for document-grounded answers. Show sources where possible. Do not store secrets. Let users inspect and delete memory. Save intermediate outputs in workflows. Test safe and unsafe inputs. Be honest about limitations. ## 10.34 Mini Challenges ### Challenge 1: Add a Risk Score Modify RiskAssessment to include a numeric score: 0 = low risk 1 = medium risk 2 = high risk Then display it in the app. ### Challenge 2: Add a Source Requirement Validator Create a validator that checks whether a RAG answer includes: Source: Page: This helps enforce citations in document assistants. ### Challenge 3: Add a Sensitive Memory Blocker Reuse looks_like_secret() in your Chapter 7 memory assistant. Block memory that appears to contain secrets. ### Challenge 4: Add Tool Approval Before running any external tool, ask: This action requires approval. Continue? yes/no ### Challenge 5: Add a Guarded Email Drafter Create a mode where the assistant can draft emails but always includes: Review before sending. ### Challenge 6: Add a Guardrail Log Log risky requests to: guardrail_events.log Do not log secrets or private data. ## 10.35 Chapter Summary In this chapter, you added a professional safety layer to your AI applications. You learned that guardrails can check inputs, validate outputs, and require human review before risky actions. You built a guarded assistant that can: Detect possible secrets Block destructive requests Trigger review for external actions Trigger review for sensitive advice Validate model output Create human review checklists Reduce risky behavior with safer prompts Guardrails do not make an AI app perfect. But they make it more responsible, more trustworthy, and more ready for real users. In the next chapter, you will continue strengthening your AI systems by learning testing, evaluation, monitoring, and cost control. Because a serious AI app is not finished when it works once. It is ready when it works reliably. ## Key Takeaways Guardrails are checks that help AI apps behave more safely and reliably. Hallucinations are confident but unsupported or false outputs. Input guardrails check user messages before model calls. Output guardrails validate responses before showing them. Action guardrails protect external or irreversible actions. Human review is essential for sensitive or client-facing workflows. RAG reduces hallucinations but does not eliminate them. Tool-using agents need allowlists and approval gates.
